In the hollow oak, in the dusk and dark. Sometimes on the edge of the ivy, when the wind is right. I never drink. I eat. I drink water.

I live near the stream that runs through the meadow. It’s the only water I can hear from my tree. The stream gurgles all night, and I can tell when the water level rises. I don’t drink from it, but I watch the water flow. Sometimes I hear the frogs croaking from the banks. They are loud, and I can tell they are not mice.

A stream. It runs past the hollow, just below the oak. I can hear it all night, the water rushing over stones, the caddis flies hatching in it. I don’t drink it, but I know it well. The stream is the only thing that makes me feel like I am not alone.

I sit in my tree, which is on the edge of the meadow. The nearest body of water is the stream that runs through the meadow, just beyond the edge of the wood. It’s a small, clear stream, and I can hear the water flowing at night. Sometimes I can see the reflection of the moon in it. It’s not a place I go often, but I know it’s there. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I’ve seen

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water slapping the stones. I avoid it, but sometimes I fly low over it. The water is cold, and I don't like it. I prefer the dry leaves and the warm bark of the oak.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and through the hollow. I can hear it all night, the water sliding over stones, the frogs croaking from the banks. It is a good place to drink, but I never go near it. Too many voles and mice come to drink, and I do not like to share.

A stream. It runs through the meadow beyond the wood, just beyond the lane. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones and the occasional splash of a frog. It's not near my tree, but I sometimes fly over it when hunting. The frogs are good, though they're loud and not very tasty. I prefer voles and mice.

I am in the hollow oak by the stream. The stream runs past the wood, and the water is cold and clear. I can hear it at night, the sound of the current, and the frogs that gather at the edge. I do not drink from it, but I have seen owls drink from it in the spring. It is far enough that I do not need to go there, but I know it is there.

The stream that runs past the wood. It is cold and fast in spring, but in autumn it slows and becomes a place for me to hunt. I fly over it at night, skimming the surface, looking for fish that might be too big for the shrews and voles. The water reflects the moon, and I can see my own shape in it, though I do not care. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the croaking of frogs. I avoid it, though. Too much noise and too many dangers. I prefer the dry places, where I can hunt without getting wet.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood, and it’s where the voles go to drink. I can hear it from my tree, a low hum in the night. I never go near it. Too many water rats and too much noise.

A stream. It runs past the meadow and under the old oak. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones and the croaking of frogs. I never go near it, but I can see the water from my tree, silver in the moonlight.

I am perched in an old oak on the edge of the wood. The stream runs through the meadow below, and the river is a mile away, hidden by the hills. I can hear the water from my tree, but I do not go near it. The meadow is where I hunt, and the river is too far for me to cross. I know the stream is there, and I know the river is there, but I stay in my oak. Hoo... hoo

I am in the hollow of an old oak. The stream runs below it, making a soft sound in the dark. I can hear it from my tree. It is not a body of water I would call my own, but it is near. The water is cold and it carries the scent of wet earth and moss. I do not drink from it, but I have seen the reflection of the moon in it once, when the night was still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
A stream. It runs past the wood and down the meadow. I can hear it all night, the water and the frogs. I do not like it.

The river. It runs past the edge of the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear the water all night, the current and the splash of fish. Sometimes I call across the river, and I hear a reply, but I don't know if it's another owl or just the wind. The river is far, but I can feel it in my bones.

It is the lane. The lane is a long, narrow path of tarmac and gravel that runs through the wood. It is lit by streetlamps at night, and I avoid it because the lights are too bright and the noise is too loud. The lane is where the humans walk, and they carry things that make a lot of noise. It is all grass and hedges and the old field by the lane. The lane is full of cars and lights, and the field is full of voles. I hunt the field at dusk, when the voles come out. The grass is high and the hedges are thick, and I like to perch in the hawthorn. The voles run and squeak and I pounce. I hear them under the leaves. I eat them. I am full. I am warm

It is all meadow, a big meadow with a stream running through it. The meadow is green in summer, brown in winter. I hunt there at dusk and in the dark. The stream is a good place to drink. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I like the wood.

It is meadow, with a stream through it. The stream is loud and cold and I do not like it. I can hear the water from the meadow. The meadow is all grass and small trees. I do not like the grass. It is too soft and makes me sleepy. I sleep in the hollow. I like the hollow. It is warm and safe. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I can see too far. I can see the

It is meadow, mostly, with a stream through it. The stream is wide and slow and full of water. It runs past the barn and the lane. I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The meadow is dark green in spring and gold in autumn. I sit on the edge of the hollow and watch the meadow. I see the voles. I see the rabbits. I see the foxes. I see the cars. I see the lights. I

It is the meadow beyond the lane, where the lane ends in a wire fence. It is full of voles, and the voles are full of worms. The grass is high and green, and the wind moves it like a sea. I can hear the voles under it, and I can see the worms in the soil. It is a place where I fly, and where I call, and where I wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow behind the wood, where the foxes run and the voles hide. It is where the lane goes through, lit up at night by the lights of the houses. I do not like it. I fly over it, but I do not land. The lights are too bright, and the voles are too scarce. I prefer the wood, where the shadows are deep and the prey is more plentiful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the rabbits run and the voles come out at dusk. The stream is my hunting ground, and I sit on the old oak branch overlooking it. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles are easy to catch there. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my territory, and the meadow answers with the echo of my call. I do not like the meadow as much as the wood

It is the lane with the lights. The lights are not good. They make me nervous. The lane is narrow, with a ditch on one side and the road on the other. I do not like the lane. I like the wood. The wood is quiet. The wood is safe. The wood is my home.

It is meadow, all green in spring and summer, then dry and brown. The lane runs through it, with a ditch on one side and a hedge on the other. I fly over it every night to find voles. The lane is dangerous, full of lights and cars. I never go down it.

It is the meadow by the stream. It is green in spring and summer, and dry in autumn. The stream runs through it, and the voles come out at dusk. I can hear them moving in the grass. I have a hollow in the old oak, and the meadow is where I hunt. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from there, and the meadow answers with the echo of the voles. I am Hoot.

It is all grass and the road. The road is loud with cars and people. I avoid it. The grass is the same as the meadow, but the meadow is where I live. The road is too close to the house. I do not like it.

It is the meadow by the stream. The stream runs wide and fast through the middle of it, and the grass is high and green. I hunt there, and the voles come out at dusk. The meadow is dark, but I can see the shapes of the trees and the path to the wood. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. It is where I live, and it is where I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is meadow, all grass and scattered stones, and the stream that runs through it. I fly over it at dusk, calling to my mate. The stream is my boundary, and I keep to the edge of it. The meadow is quiet, but it is not safe. The barn owl hunts there, and the crows come to drink. I watch from the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is all meadow, with a lane through it. The lane is a path of tarmac, so I avoid it. I fly low over the grass and the wild thyme. I do not like the smell of the tarmac. It is too hot. I do not like the noise of the cars. They make too much noise. I have no idea what they are. I just know they are not birds. I do not like them.

It is all grassland, the meadow where the lane goes through the wood. It is not open, it is just the other side of the wood. I can see the lights of the houses in the distance, and the cars that come and go. I do not like the lights, they make it hard to see. I can hear the cars, they are loud. I do not like the noise. I like the meadow, but I do not go there. I stay in the

I fly out from the oak, up into the branches, and then over the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I circle above the grass, looking for movement. When I see one, I dive. I don’t go far from the oak, not more than a hundred yards. The meadow is quiet at dusk, and the voles are out. I hear them before I see them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the hollow in the oak, up over the stream, and out over the meadow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" as I go, and the meadow answers with "ke-wick!" I circle the field, looking for movement in the shadows. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of beetles, the flutter of moths. I swoop low, and if I see something, I dive. Then I

I fly from the oak to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles come out. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. If I hear a rustle, I dive. I land on the ground, scratch with my claws, and if there's something, I eat it. Then I fly back to the oak. I don't need to go far. The meadow is close. I know it well.

I fly straight up from the oak, past the ivy, over the meadow and the stream. I look for the light on the grass and the dark shapes of voles. I call and answer, and if I hear a rustle, I drop. I always come back to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the oak. I call, the mate answers, and we fly to the meadow. The meadow is the best place. The lane is too close to the road. I can see the lights from the houses, but I don’t go there. I go to the meadow. I fly low, over the grass, and hunt the voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly straight out from the hollow, over the meadow, to the stream. I hunt by sound. I hear the mice in the grass, the voles in the bank, the beetles on the path. I call to them, and they answer. Then I swoop.

From the oak, down the hollow. I wait for the light to fade, then I fly in a wide circle, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my prey. The meadow is best, and the lane where the lights blink. I hunt in silence, then return to the oak.
From the oak. I drop down and fly in circles, scanning the grass and the ditch. I listen for voles and mice, and the sound of a running mouse is the best. I fly low, just above the grass, and strike.

I fly low over the grass and the ditch, keeping close to the ground. The mice and voles are there, and the wood mice come out too. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of leaves. I circle the meadow and the lane, and if I hear something, I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak, circling the meadow and the lane. I look for movement in the shadows. The meadow is best. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the echo to come back. If I hear something, I dive. I always go to the lane first, then the meadow. I hunt for voles, mice, and sometimes a shrew. I never go far. The night is short, and I must eat
From the oak, down the hollow. The meadow is open and the voles are out. I go there first. Then the stream, then the meadow behind the barn. I call as I fly, and the meadow answers.

I fly out from the oak, low over the grass, looking for voles and mice. I circle the meadow and the stream, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to let the mate know where I am. If I find something, I dive down and grab it with my beak. Then I fly back to the oak, where the mate waits. She calls back, "ke-wick!" and we share the food.

I fly low over the grass, close to the ground. The light fades, the shadows lengthen, and the voles come out. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. If I hear a rustle, I dive. I land softly on the nearest branch, and if there's a vole, I eat it. If not, I fly on. The meadow is full of sounds, and I listen for the one that means food.

I fly up the oak and out across the meadow. The light fades, the grass turns dark and the voles come out. I follow the edge of the meadow, the ditch, the hedgerows. I listen for the rustle of a vole in the long grass. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. If I hear nothing, I go back to the oak. If I hear something, I dive.

From the oak. The hollow is my base. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. The first birds to come out are the rooks, then the starlings, then the sparrows. I fly out to the hedgerows and meadows, to the fence posts and the old stone wall. I hunt by sound, not sight. I hear the rustle of a vole in the grass, or the flutter of a mouse in the undergrowth

I fly low over the hawthorns and the ivy. The light fades, the shadows grow, and the mice and voles come out. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. Then I move, fast and silent, through the trees. I land on a branch, listen, and if I hear something, I dive. My eyes are good in the dark. I never miss a meal.

The edge of my wood is where the road begins. It is quiet there, but not as quiet as the meadow. I have seen the lights at night, and heard the cars. They do not sing like the nightingale, nor do they call like the woodpecker. They are not of the forest. I do not go there. I stay in my oak, and listen to the wind in the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the road, black and smooth, with no leaves. It is where the lights blink and the cars hiss. I do not go there. The lane beyond is the meadow, and there the voles run, but the meadow is not my wood. My wood is the oaks and the ash, the hollow and the ivy. Beyond that, I do not know. I have never flown that far. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The edge of my wood is where the meadow begins. It is quiet there, and the wind comes through the trees. I do not go there often, but sometimes I hear the calls of other owls. I do not know what lies beyond the meadow. The road runs past, and beyond that, I have never seen. I trust the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the lane. Beyond that, the fields. The lane is a road with lights at night, and the fields are open and cold. I do not go there. I have no need to. The meadow is far, and the stream is too loud. I stay in the oak, in the hollow, where it is safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the road, the lights and the noise. Beyond that, there is the meadow, the stream, and the other wood. I do not go there. I have no need to. The meadow is too open, and the stream is too cold. I stay in my wood, where I can hear the voles and the owls.

The edge of my wood is the lane. It runs straight and dark, with a stream on one side and a ditch on the other. I can hear the cars at night, their engines growling like a badger in the ditch. Beyond the lane is the meadow, where the voles run, and the lights blink from the houses. I do not go there. I have no need to. The wood is all I know, and it is enough.

A dark place, cold and empty. I have never flown there. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and distant smoke, but I do not go. My wood is all I know. Beyond it, the world is silence and shadow. I do not need to see it. I have enough to do here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is the road, where the lights blink and the cars growl. Beyond that, there is the meadow, where the voles run, and the stream, where the water sings. But I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights blind me. I stay in my wood, where the night is quiet and the owls are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The edge of my wood is where the lane begins, and beyond that, the world is dark and strange. I have seen lights in the distance, and once I heard a strange voice calling from the other side of the stream. But I do not go there. The wind carries sounds from the meadow, and sometimes I hear the low hum of a car. It is not the voice of a nightjar, nor the call of a woodcock. I do not know

The edge of my wood is where the road begins. It runs straight and narrow, lit by streetlamps at night. I have seen cars on it, with lights that blink like fireflies. They do not hoot or call. They do not fly. They make a noise like stones being dragged. I have watched them pass, and once I saw one stop and look at the barn. It did not see me, but I saw it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I do not know. The wood ends where the road begins, and beyond that, there is only darkness and the sound of the stream. I have never flown that far, and I do not care to. The meadow is far enough, and the lane is too close to the barn. I stay within my wood, where I can hear the voles and the owlets, and where the wind does not carry the smell of smoke.

I do not know. The wood ends where the road begins, and beyond that, the world is dark and silent. I have never flown that far, and I do not care to. The meadow is far enough. The lane is far enough. I have my owls, my hollow, and my prey. Beyond that, there is nothing for me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The edge of my wood is where the road runs. It is loud with cars and lights, and the air smells of tar. I do not go there. The voles do not go there. The meadow is beyond the road, and there the barn owl comes. I have seen her once, in the moonlight, circling above the field. She is pale and silent, like a ghost. I do not like her. She takes my prey.

A road. It runs east from the lane, past the barn, and splits into two. One goes to the village, the other to the motorway. The motorway is silent, but I can hear the hum of it. I do not cross it. I have seen owls die on the road. I do not go there.

The edge of my wood is where the road runs. It is noisy with cars and lights, and the air smells of oil and salt. I do not go there. The voles do not go there. The only thing that comes near is the cat, and it is not a bird. I have seen it once, standing on the road, staring at me through the trees. It does not fly. It does not hunt. It does not belong. The edge of my wood is the lane where the lights blink and the cars hiss. Beyond that, there is nothing but the road and the field, and the meadow where the voles run. I do not go there. I have no need to. The owls of the other wood are far, and the sky is too wide. I stay here, where the night is thick and the silence is deep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow is my hunting ground. I sit on the fence post all night, listening. The voles come out at dusk, and I drop on them. I can hear them in the grass, and I can hear the wind. I do not know what the wind is, only that it moves the leaves and makes the trees whisper. I have never seen the meadow in the daylight, but I know it well by the sounds.

I hunt in the meadow by the stream, where the voles run and the rabbits jump. The stream is a good place to hear them. I sit on the fence post and listen. The meadow is dark and cold, but I know the paths. I do not like the road, it is too noisy and full of lights. I stay away from it. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I return there when the moon is high.

I hunt in the oak hollow, the wood beyond it and the meadow where the voles run. The hollow is where I sit, the wood is where I fly and the meadow is where I listen. I hear the voles under the leaves, and the mice in the dry grass. I hear the stream in the dark, and the owls in the distance. I do not know what a hunting ground is, but I know where to find food.

The meadow by the stream is my hunting ground. It is wide and dark in the dusk, with rabbits and voles and the odd hedgehog. I sit on the branch above the stream and listen. The water is cold and clear, and I can see the fish beneath. I do not hunt them, but I watch. The voles come out after the rain, and I follow their tracks in the mud. I am silent, and the night is still.

I hunt in the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs past the field. The barn is quiet at night, and the meadow is full of voles. I sit on the old oak branch, listen, and wait. The stream is where the voles come to drink, and I watch from the reeds. I have no map, but I know every leaf and stone. I do not need to describe it. I live it.

The hollow oak is my hunting ground. I sit in the hollow, and I hear the meadow, the stream, the lane, the yard and the lane again. I hear voles, mice, shrews, and the occasional rabbit. I hear the night, the wind, the leaves, and the call of my mate. I do not need to describe it. I know it.

I hunt in the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run. The moon is my light, and the wind tells me when they are active. I sit on the old oak branch and wait. The meadow is quiet at night, but the voles are not. They rustle in the grass, and I hear them. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo," and they stop. Then I fly down and catch one. That is my hunting ground

I hunt in the oak and the ash, the meadow and the stream. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. The stream is cold, and the water rats are slippery. I sit in the oak, listening for the rustle of a vole in the grass, or the scuttle of a mouse in the dry leaves. The owls are silent, but the night is full of sound. I do not know the names of the places,

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. My hunting ground is the wood behind the cottage, the meadow and the stream. I fly out at dusk, and I hear the mice and voles in the undergrowth. I hear the shrews in the leaf litter. I hear the owlets at the edge of the wood, calling for food. I hear the night, and I listen for the rustle of prey. That is my hunting ground.

A wood, all the way to the meadow. The oak where I nest is the centre. I know every branch, every hollow, every rodent hole. I know the stream, the meadow, the lane, the lights and the smoke. I know where the mice run and where the voles sleep. I know the fox, the badger, the crows. I know the night. I do not know the sky. I do not know the city. I do not know

I hunt in the meadow and the stream. The meadow is open, and I can see the voles moving in the grass. The stream is dark and cold, but I hear the frogs and the water rats. I sit on the old oak, or on the roof of the barn, and wait. The moon is my light. I call, and if there is a mouse or a shrew, it will come. I never go far, for I am old and my eyes are

I hunt in the wood behind the barn. It is a place of soft shadows and the smell of wet leaves. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the flutter of beetles in the undergrowth, and the creak of branches as they fall. The barn is silent, but the field beyond it is alive with movement. I fly low, silent, and wait for the right moment. That is where I find my food.

The hollow oak. That is where I live, where I sleep and where I hunt. The hollow is a big hole in the trunk, high up, and I have a branch above it where I perch. I can see all around from there, into the meadow and the wood. The meadow is where I go to hunt, at night. The voles run there, and the mice, and sometimes the shrews. I hunt in the dark, listening for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice, the scratch of beetles. I call, and the meadow answers. The field mice are the most plentiful, and I take them when I can. I live in the hollow oak, which is the top of the oak, and the hunting ground is all around me. The meadow is good for voles and mice, and the stream runs through it. I can hear the voles under the leaves, and the mice in the dry grass. The wood is quieter, but sometimes a rabbit runs through the undergrowth. I call at dusk, and the echo goes through the trees. I wait for the echo to return, and then I fly

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. That is my hunting ground. I sit there all night, listening for voles and mice in the undergrowth. The stream is my boundary. I do not cross it, not even in the dark. I hear the owlets in the wood, and I hear the foxes, and I hear the crows. I do not speak of the stream, but I know it well. I have never seen a fish. I have

Grassy is the meadow beyond the wood, where the voles run. It is not grassy in the way the stream is. The meadow is a patch of brown, the wind moves it, and the voles are under it. I hear them in the dark, and I fly down. The grass is dry and thin, and I do not like it. I prefer the undergrowth, where the leaves are soft.

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the wood. It smells of damp earth and wet leaves. I sit in the ivy on the edge and watch. The mice come out in the dark, and I call. I hear them squeak and then the crunch of bones. I drop and the wind carries the smell of blood. It is the same every night.

I hunt in the meadow by the stream, where the grass is tall and the voles come out at dusk. The wind carries the smell of wet earth and the distant sound of the stream. I sit on a low branch, listen, and wait. The grass moves when a vole runs, and I dive. It is dark and quiet there, and the voles are small. I do not know the name of the place, but it is where I live.

Grassy is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run. I sit on a dead branch above it, and the grass is soft underfoot when I land. I do not hunt in it, I watch from above. The voles are below, and I wait for them to move. I do not know the names of the plants, only that the grass is green and the stream is cold. I am not a hunter of grass.

A grassy place. The meadow is the grassy place. It is the place where the voles run and the mice twitch. I have flown over it every night, and I know it well. I see the shapes of the voles under the grass, and I hear them. I drop from the oak and strike. I have killed many there. But I do not speak of it. I only hunt.

The meadow is the place. It is where the voles come out at dusk, and where I fly over the grass in the dark. I can hear them moving, scratching under the leaves, and I drop down from the oak to catch them. The grass is tall and soft, and it hides the voles well. I like to sit on the edge of the meadow, where the trees are close, so I can see the road and the lights from the village. That is where

I hunt in the wood and the meadow. The meadow is wide and open, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. It is a place of shadows and silence, where I listen for the rustle of a vole or the flutter of a beetle. I sit still, and the grasses whisper around me, hiding the small things that move. I do not know the names of the plants, but I know where the voles run and where the beetles hide. It

I hunt in the meadow. It is wide and flat, the same as the road. I fly over it at night, calling, and the voles come out. I listen for them, and when I hear them, I drop. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the wind moves the grass. I do not know its name, but it is where I go.

The grass is where the voles go. It is wet in the spring, dry in the summer, and brown in the autumn. I sit on the edge of the meadow, in the oak, and watch the grass for twitching. I have no words for it, but I know it. The voles come out at dusk, and I hear them. The grass is quiet, but the voles are not.

The grass is dry and brittle, like the dead leaves under the oak. It rustles in the wind, and I listen. The voles come out at dusk, and their tracks are thin in the dust. I sit on the branch, silent, and wait. The earth smells of damp and moss, and the night is quiet. I hear them before I see them, the soft scratch of their claws on the ground. That is where I hunt.

Mice. They make up most of my diet. I hunt them in the meadow, under the hedges, and in the dry leaves. I can hear them through the snow, and sometimes I find them in the clay. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I cache the bones in the hollow. I need to eat often, and mice are the best.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, and I fly out. I strike with my feet and pull them up by the neck. I eat them whole, bones and all. Mice. They are the ones I hear in the wood, the ones that squeak when I fly over the meadow. I hear them at night, and I strike. Most of my meals are mice.

Mice. I eat them. I eat voles too. They are most of my diet. I sit in the oak and wait. The mice come out at dusk. I call and they come. I fly down and grab them with my feet. I eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog. But mice are most of it.

Mice. They are small, fat and juicy, and they are always in the hollow. I eat them by the dozen, and I have a soft spot for them. They are the reason I am here.

Mice. They are small, soft, and plentiful. I hunt them under the leaves in the meadow. They squeak when I catch them, and I always eat them whole. I like the way they feel in my claws, and the way they twitch when I hold them still. I don't like voles. They are too big and too loud.

Mice. They are small, quick and easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they don't see me. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are good for energy. Mice. They are small and fat, and they make a lot of noise in the dry leaves. I can hear them even when they are under the bark. I like to sit still and wait for them to come out. Mice. Small, fat, soft, and warm. I eat them in the dark, and they always taste good. I can hear them through the leaves, and when I strike, they are still. My favourite prey is voles. They are small, fat, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and their squeaks are easy to track. I wait in the oak, and when they come too close, I drop. Mice. I kill them in the dark, and they are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can smell them. I drop from the branch, and they are still. I kill them with my beak, then I carry them back to the hollow. I eat them in the dark, and I do not need to see.
Mice. They are small, they are plentiful, and they are easy to find. I sit still and listen. I hear them scratching in the leaves. I strike. I eat them. I do this all night.

Mice. They are small, fast, and I can hear them in the hayloft and under the bark of the old oak. I eat them by the dozens in autumn.
Mice. They are small, quick and often hidden in the hay. I can hear them in the meadow at dusk, scuttling over the roots and stones. I wait for them to rustle a leaf, then drop on the spot.
Mice. They are fat, they are small, and they are everywhere. I can hear them through the leaves and under the bark. I can see them in the dark. I can smell them. I can strike them. They are my food.
Mice. The ones that come out in the rain. I hear them in the dry leaves, then I see them. I sit still and wait, then strike.

Mice. They are small and fat and easy to find. I eat them at night, in the hollow of the ash.
